parties:
Anwar Hossain Mintu ----- Convict Petitioner
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
A.M. Mahmudur Rahman, J: In this petition under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh the question mooted at the bar is: whether the order of conviction and sentence passed by the Special Tribunal under the Special Powers Act, 1974 can be declared as to have been passed without lawful authority and be of no legal effect without having recourse to the provision of section 30 of the Special Powers Act within the statutory period of limitation. 

 7. It is extraneously argued at the bar that alternative remedy is no bar to Article 102 of the Constitution. Although mere alternative remedy does not always defeat the writ of certiorari but the question before us is: whether such relief can be had on the facts of the present case? Presently we will answer. The Special Powers Act is a special enactment and it deals with certain offences unlike the general laws. The makers of the enactment were conscious about the existence of the Law of Limitation. Therefore, in enacting this law the makers of the law having had before them the Limitation Act did not apply the provisions of the said Act for nothing. It was a conscious omission on the part of the Parliament not to apply section 5 of the Limitation Act to a case which stand barred by limitation under section 30 of the Special Powers Act. 

 8. Now it brings us to the second question: whether because of limitation the petitioner is not entitled to the jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution. Article 102 of the Constitution applies where a person performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority has done or taken any act without lawful authority. In order to apply Article 102 of the Constitution we have to look at the language used therein. The foundation for the declaration as the petitioner wants to have from us is founded on the expression "without lawful authority". In this case as the Special Tribunal was constituted under the Special Powers Act, 1974 we do not find want of any lawful authority in passing the impugned judgment and order by the tribunal. Therefore, the petitioner is not entitled, upon the facts of the present case, to have remedy under Article 102 of the Constitution and in our opinion, on the facts of case, this alternative remedy under S. 30 of the Special Powers Act, 1974 acts as a bar to the petition under Article 102 of the Constitution. The remedy under Article 102 of the Constitution is a discretionary remedy and this Division in a proper case has discretion torefuse the grant of any writ if it finds that there was alternative and efficacious remedy provided in the Code and in that case the high prerogative writ should not be utilised as a substitute of ordinary remedies.
